LLM agents must fit tool schemas, documents, examples, notes and history into a token budget. Common heuristics (relevance, coverage, compression, fixed priorities) do not measure how much each kind of context changes task success. We introduce marginal context value (MCV) profiles: per model and task family, the expected success drop when a context type is removed, the value of its short variant, and pairwise type interactions. Each is estimated once by counterfactual ablation with bootstrap intervals and a length-neutral control. A CP-SAT compiler selects blocks under the budget, with dependencies and variants, in milliseconds without calling the language model. In a pre-registered, fully local evaluation on Qwen3-4B-Instruct (multi-hop QA over HotpotQA, BFCL tool calling, long-history recall) against six baselines including LLMLingua-2 and a coverage selector, the primary hypothesis failed. MCV did not significantly exceed embedding relevance in area under the success-budget curve in any family, and trailed it by 0.053 on history, where its block ranker favored recent over relevant sessions. The efficiency hypothesis, added after development pilots but before any test run, held in two of three families: at an 8k budget MCV sent 34.9% fewer prompt tokens on tool calling and 6.9% fewer on history with non-inferior success; since full contexts are shorter than 8k tokens, this measures pruning rather than budgeted selection. Interaction terms had no effect. The 4B profiles showed that worked examples carried little individual value, and Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B type values agreed (rho = 0.88 over 7 pooled pairs); on Qwen3-8B a transferred profile gave the same outcome as a natively measured one in every paired episode, which also indicates low sensitivity of the compiler to the type profile. Code and logs of every model call are released.
